sections.title: The cups are close, but the arms do not reach out
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A figure sits on a slope beneath a tree, arms folded, legs crossed and head slightly lowered. A green outer garment covers red sleeves, with the trunk directly behind. Three golden cups stand on the grass in front; a hand emerges from a cloud on the left to offer a fourth.

All four cups remain upright. The figure neither takes one nor knocks one away. Low shrubs and distant hills appear behind. A withdrawn posture alongside continuing offers from outside is visible in the picture. Whether the person is resting, hesitating or rejecting the offer still requires interpretation; posture alone cannot decide it. [View the card image](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cups04.jpg)

sections.title: Dissatisfaction in the text and new relationships in the reversal
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The 1911 English transcription of Waite’s The Pictorial Key to the Tarot describes dissatisfaction with the surroundings, using weariness, aversion and boredom after satiety to explain the upright card. The wording is judgemental and should not be applied directly to someone who is exhausted. [Waite’s entry for this card](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktcu04.htm)

The historical reversed entry names novelty, new instruction and new relationships. This article therefore treats renewed attention to the outside world as its main reversed theme. Using the upright card to identify needs and preserve choice is this site’s modern extension.

sections.title: Upright: Ask why you do not want it
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Lack of interest may mean too much is being asked of you, or that the available options do not fit. Notice whether everything feels tiring or only this particular kind of arrangement. Then decide whether to rest, decline or try something different.

A pause is useful when you know what you will observe afterwards. Allow a defined period of recovery, then revisit the options. That makes changes in your needs easier to see than endlessly saying you will think about it later.

sections.title: Reversed: Let interest return gradually
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The reversal can suggest willingness to reconnect: a short meeting, a trial class or a closer look at an offer you set aside. New interest need not immediately become a long-term plan. Ask for details before deciding how much to commit.

If fear of missing out is driving a string of yeses, more activity may not bring more enjoyment. Small trials you can leave help you understand yourself while keeping renewed participation separate from renewed exhaustion.

sections.title: Assessing opportunities and invitations
sections.bodyMarkdown:
If a colleague invites you into a project, ask how much time it needs and what the tasks involve. You may be resisting an undefined burden rather than the project itself. With better information, you can still decline or propose a smaller contribution.

If you do not want to socialise on a day off, say you would like some quiet time. If you miss your friends a few weeks later, start with a short walk. If nothing seems interesting in creative work, step away from reference material and record one thing in daily life that genuinely catches your attention.

sections.title: Practice: Make the refusal specific
sections.bodyMarkdown: Choose one invitation or plan you have set aside. Write what it actually asks of you, why you are unwilling, and which change would make you reconsider. If no change would make you want it, a clear refusal is also a completed decision.

sections.title: A common misreading
sections.bodyMarkdown: The Four of Cups cannot label someone lazy, cold or mentally ill, and every offered cup need not be a precious opportunity. The image can help you ask questions. If physical or emotional difficulties continue to interfere with daily life, real support and suitable professional assessment matter.

sections.title: Read alongside
sections.bodyMarkdown: Ace of Cups: Compare willingness to receive with a temporary lack of interest; Eight of Cups: Distinguish a short pause from a decision to leave.

articleMarkdown:
# Four of Cups Meaning: Understand why nothing appeals

In one sentence: When a new offer leaves you cold, first work out whether you need rest or change.

Card: Four of Cups  
Rank: IV · RWS Minor Arcana · Cups  
Keywords: Pause · Weariness · Renewed attention

Upright at a glance: You may not want anything new for now. Allow time to observe and identify your needs.  
Reversed at a glance: Interest in the outside world may be returning. Try taking part in one small thing.

Even when someone offers an opportunity, you may want to say, “Another time.” The Four of Cups does not hurry you into saying yes. It asks what your refusal is protecting right now.

## The cups are close, but the arms do not reach out

A figure sits on a slope beneath a tree, arms folded, legs crossed and head slightly lowered. A green outer garment covers red sleeves, with the trunk directly behind. Three golden cups stand on the grass in front; a hand emerges from a cloud on the left to offer a fourth.

All four cups remain upright. The figure neither takes one nor knocks one away. Low shrubs and distant hills appear behind. A withdrawn posture alongside continuing offers from outside is visible in the picture. Whether the person is resting, hesitating or rejecting the offer still requires interpretation; posture alone cannot decide it. [View the card image](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cups04.jpg)

## Dissatisfaction in the text and new relationships in the reversal

The 1911 English transcription of Waite’s The Pictorial Key to the Tarot describes dissatisfaction with the surroundings, using weariness, aversion and boredom after satiety to explain the upright card. The wording is judgemental and should not be applied directly to someone who is exhausted. [Waite’s entry for this card](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktcu04.htm)

The historical reversed entry names novelty, new instruction and new relationships. This article therefore treats renewed attention to the outside world as its main reversed theme. Using the upright card to identify needs and preserve choice is this site’s modern extension.

## Upright: Ask why you do not want it

Lack of interest may mean too much is being asked of you, or that the available options do not fit. Notice whether everything feels tiring or only this particular kind of arrangement. Then decide whether to rest, decline or try something different.

A pause is useful when you know what you will observe afterwards. Allow a defined period of recovery, then revisit the options. That makes changes in your needs easier to see than endlessly saying you will think about it later.

## Reversed: Let interest return gradually

The reversal can suggest willingness to reconnect: a short meeting, a trial class or a closer look at an offer you set aside. New interest need not immediately become a long-term plan. Ask for details before deciding how much to commit.

If fear of missing out is driving a string of yeses, more activity may not bring more enjoyment. Small trials you can leave help you understand yourself while keeping renewed participation separate from renewed exhaustion.

## Assessing opportunities and invitations

If a colleague invites you into a project, ask how much time it needs and what the tasks involve. You may be resisting an undefined burden rather than the project itself. With better information, you can still decline or propose a smaller contribution.

If you do not want to socialise on a day off, say you would like some quiet time. If you miss your friends a few weeks later, start with a short walk. If nothing seems interesting in creative work, step away from reference material and record one thing in daily life that genuinely catches your attention.

## Practice: Make the refusal specific

Choose one invitation or plan you have set aside. Write what it actually asks of you, why you are unwilling, and which change would make you reconsider. If no change would make you want it, a clear refusal is also a completed decision.

## A common misreading

The Four of Cups cannot label someone lazy, cold or mentally ill, and every offered cup need not be a precious opportunity. The image can help you ask questions. If physical or emotional difficulties continue to interfere with daily life, real support and suitable professional assessment matter.

## Read alongside

Ace of Cups: Compare willingness to receive with a temporary lack of interest; Eight of Cups: Distinguish a short pause from a decision to leave.

sourceRecord.oneLineSummary: 面对新的提议提不起劲时，先弄清自己是需要休息还是需要改变。
sourceRecord.uprightQuickTake: 暂时不想接新东西，给自己一点观察与辨认需要的时间。

sourceRecord.hook: 明明有人递来机会，你却只想说改天吧。圣杯四不催你马上点头，它让你看一看：此刻的拒绝，究竟在保护什么。

sections.title: 杯子在附近，手臂却没有伸出去
paragraphs: 人物坐在树下的斜坡上，双臂交抱、双腿盘起，头部微低。绿色外衣覆在红袖上，树干就在背后；面前草地上摆着三只金杯，左侧一团云伸出手，送来第四只杯。
四只杯都保持直立，人物没有去拿，也没有把任何一只推倒。背景可见低矮树丛与远山。身体收拢，外界仍在提供事物，这种距离是画面可以直接观察的；他究竟在休息、犹豫还是嫌弃，仍需要解释，不能只凭姿势断定。 [查看本篇牌面](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cups04.jpg)

sections.title: 原文的不满与逆位的新关系
paragraphs: Waite《塔罗图解之钥》1911 英文转录把人物描述为对环境不满，并用厌倦、反感和饱足后的无趣解释正位。他的措辞带有责备意味，不能直接拿来评价正在疲惫的人。 [Waite 本牌原文](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktcu04.htm)
原文逆位列出新事物、新教导与新关系，因此本篇以重新留意外界作为逆位主线。正位也可以用于辨认需求与保留选择，这一部分属于本站的现代延伸。

sections.title: 正位 先问为什么不想要
paragraphs: 提不起兴趣可能来自负荷太大，也可能是现有选项不适合。先分清自己对所有事情都累，还是只对这一类安排没兴趣，再决定休息、拒绝或换一种尝试。
暂停有价值，但最好知道暂停后要观察什么。给自己一段明确的休整时间，随后重新看选项；比不断说以后再说，更容易发现需求有没有变化。

sections.title: 逆位 允许兴趣一点点回来
paragraphs: 逆位可读作愿意重新接触：接受一场短会面、试一节课、认真看一眼之前搁下的提议。新的兴趣不必一出现就变成长期计划，可以先问细节，再决定是否投入。
如果只是因为怕错过而乱答应，忙起来也未必更有感觉。用可退出的小尝试了解自己，让恢复参与与透支自己保持区别。

sections.title: 面对机会和邀请时怎么判断
paragraphs: 同事邀请你加入新项目，先问需要多少时间、任务内容是什么。你拒绝的可能是模糊负担，而不是项目本身；掌握信息后，可以继续拒绝，也可以提出较小的参与范围。
休息日不想参加聚会，直接说明想安静待一会儿。若几周后开始想念朋友，先约一次短散步。创作时看什么都觉得没意思，也可以暂时离开参考资料，记录生活里一件真实吸引注意的小事。

sections.title: 练习 把不想要写清楚
paragraphs: 选一个被你搁置的邀请或计划，分别写下：它具体要求什么；我不愿意的原因；改变哪一个条件后我会重新考虑。若没有任何条件能让你愿意，清楚拒绝也是一个完成的决定。

sections.title: 容易看错的地方
paragraphs: 不能凭圣杯四给人贴上懒惰、冷漠或心理疾病的标签，也不必把每个递来的杯子都称作珍贵机会。图像适合帮助你提问；实际身心困扰若持续影响生活，需要现实支持与合适的专业评估。
